pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Earthquake Safety

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** Not a UK curriculum science/geography topic — earthquake drills are a Pacific-Rim/US life-skill rather than an England statutory standard. The closest UK home is PSHE/personal safety (following safety instructions, knowing a trusted adult), taught here as preparedness enrichment.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No NGSS PE covers safety drills (NGSS is science content, not preparedness). This is a preparedness/life-skill anchored on official emergency-management guidance — the internationally recommended response 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On' (USGS, FEMA/Ready.gov, Earthquake Country Alliance / Great ShakeOut).

- **Operational details:** The goal is a simple, rehearsable response, not understanding causes. Teach the three steps as a rhyme/routine — DROP to hands and knees, take COVER under a sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows if no table), and HOLD ON until the shaking stops — then tell a trusted adult. Ground the WHY in the key fact that most injuries come from falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, shelves), not from the building collapsing, so getting low and covered protects your head and neck. Explicitly teach what NOT to do: do NOT run outside (windows and exterior walls are the most dangerous place), and standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings. Practise by rehearsing the moves — real muscle memory is the point (experts stress you react faster if you've actually practised). Keep it calm and matter-of-fact; name a trusted adult to tell.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can perform Drop, Cover, Hold On on cue, say why (falling objects), and name a trusted adult; they are NOT learning earthquake causes here. Confront the dangerous myths 'run outside' and 'stand in a doorway', and reassure that most buildings do not collapse.
bestPractices: Teach the three steps as a memorable routine/rhyme (Drop → Cover → Hold On) and rehearse them physically
Ground the WHY in the key fact: most injuries are from falling/flying objects, not collapse — so get low and cover head/neck
Explicitly teach the myth-busting 'do NOT run outside' and 'a doorway is not safest' with simple reasons
Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact and reassure that most buildings do not collapse — preparedness, not fear
Always end the routine with 'tell a trusted adult' and have each child name theirs
Prioritise real physical practice (a drill) — experts note a fast response depends on having actually practised
keyRepresentations: A room scene flagging safe spots (under a sturdy table; interior wall) vs danger (windows, exterior walls, tall shelves)
A simple 'falling objects' picture showing what the cover protects against
A 'do / don't' pairing (under table vs run outside / doorway)
commonMisconceptions: 'Run outside as fast as you can' — dangerous; windows and exterior walls are the most likely to hurt you; stay put and cover
'Stand in a doorway' — outdated advice; in modern buildings a doorway is no safer and you can't brace — under a table is safer
'The main danger is the building falling down' — most injuries are from falling/flying objects; most buildings don't collapse
'Just hide anywhere' — choose a sturdy cover and hold on; not all spots are equally safe
'The safest thing is to freeze and wait' — act immediately: drop, cover, hold on the moment shaking starts

learn.summary: Earthquake safety for ages 5–7: children over-learn a simple, rehearsable response — DROP to hands and knees, take COVER under a sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows if no table), HOLD ON until shaking stops, then tell a trusted adult. The teaching objective is embodied muscle memory via a real physical drill; an on-screen timed rehearsal is a useful primer and companion but is a scaffold that teaches the sequence and reasoning, not a substitute for actually practising the moves. The 'why' is grounded in a key fact: most injuries come from falling and flying objects, not building collapse. Act immediately rather than freezing, and choose sturdy cover rather than any spot. Myths to confront calmly: do NOT run outside, and a doorway is not safest in modern buildings. Keep the tone matter-of-fact and reassuring — preparedness, not fear.

activities.title: Classroom Drop-Cover-Hold-On drill (real practice)
feedback: If a child heads for the door or outside: model that exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; stay and take cover until shaking stops

If a child goes to a doorway: explain doorways are not stronger than other parts of a modern building, do not protect you from falling or flying objects, and a swinging door could hit you — under a sturdy table is safer
If a child freezes or stays standing: act immediately — drop, cover and hold on the moment shaking starts; waiting leaves you exposed to falling objects
If a child hides somewhere that is not sturdy: choose a sturdy table or desk — not all spots give the same protection from falling objects
If a child lets go or crawls out during a pause: hold on and stay put until it's fully over — shaking can pause and restart
activities.rationale: The objective is a procedural, decision-under-pressure routine that experts say depends on having physically practised. A teacher-led drill with a real desk rehearses the actual physical moves — the dropping, crawling and holding on — that on-screen tapping does not reproduce.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: On a calm cue such as 'earthquake, drop!', physically DROP to hands and knees straight away rather than freezing
Crawl under a real, sturdy table or desk to take COVER, protecting head and neck
HOLD ON to a table leg and stay put until the teacher says the shaking has stopped
Practise staying under cover through a brief pause (shaking can start again) rather than crawling out early
When no table is available, practise moving against an interior wall away from windows and shelves and covering head/neck
After the all-clear, each child names a trusted adult they would tell, and says a short sentence they'd say
activities.intendedInsight: A fast, automatic safe response comes from having physically rehearsed the moves — act immediately, get low under sturdy cover, and protect the head and neck from falling and flying objects.

activities.title: On-screen rehearsal: the room starts to shake
feedback: Choosing to run to the window makes a lamp or vase topple harmlessly nearby (a near-miss, not scary), showing exactly why being low and covered matters
Choosing the doorway shows a gentle caption that a doorway is not the safest place in a modern building
Completing drop → cover → hold on confirms the correct sequence and offers a faster replay
activities.rationale: A timed rehearse-the-response scene teaches both the sequence and the reasoning, and primes the physical drill. Immediate consequence feedback (an object falling) makes the 'why' concrete. This is a digital primer that should point to real physical practice.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Watch a cosy room scene begin to shake, then act fast
Tap DROP so the character folds to hands and knees
Drag the character under a sturdy table to take COVER
HOLD ON as the room rattles, waiting until the shaking stops
Replay a few times to get faster at the sequence
After shaking stops, respond to the prompt 'tell a trusted adult'
activities.intendedInsight: The three steps happen in order and under time pressure; low-and-covered protects you because loose objects fall during shaking.

activities.title: Sequence and sort: safe vs not safe
feedback: If steps are out of order: re-show the routine — you get low first, then covered, then hold on until it's over
If 'run outside' is sorted as safe: exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place during shaking
If the 'why' is missed: the table protects your head and neck from falling and flying objects, which cause most injuries
activities.rationale: Sequencing and sorting assess knowledge of the steps and the myth-busting as a companion check. This format verifies recognition and recall of the procedure; it does not elicit the physical, timed response, so it complements rather than replaces the drill.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Put the three steps in order: Drop → Cover → Hold On
Sort action cards into 'safe' and 'not safe' (e.g. get under a sturdy table = safe; run outside / stand in a doorway = not safe)
Answer 'Why get under a table?' and choose the reason: to protect from falling objects
Explain in your own words why to move away from windows and shelves during shaking
activities.intendedInsight: Each safe or unsafe choice connects to a reason: get low under sturdy cover because falling and flying objects cause most injuries; don't run outside because moving during shaking can make you fall and the area near exterior walls and windows is the most dangerous place; and don't go to a doorway because in modern buildings it is no stronger than other places and does not protect you from falling or flying objects.

activities.title: Label the safe spots in the room
feedback: Tapping the window reveals that windows and exterior walls are the most dangerous place during shaking
Tapping under the sturdy table confirms it protects your head and neck from falling objects
The poster reinforces the order: drop, then cover, then hold on
activities.rationale: A labelled safe-spot scene teaches the decision and the reasons. It is a scaffold: a still, tappable image conveys where to go but cannot rehearse the timed, automatic response, so pair it with the physical drill.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Explore a room scene and tap spots flagged safe or danger
Reveal why each spot is safe (under the sturdy table) or dangerous (by the window, near tall shelves, exterior wall)
Tap through a Drop-Cover-Hold-On poster where each of the three steps animates
Point to where you would go first if the ground started shaking
activities.intendedInsight: Builds the mental map of safe vs dangerous places and the three-step routine before or alongside rehearsing it.

activities.title: Coached walk-through with a calm helper
feedback: If a child suggests running outside: the helper gently explains it's safest to stay low and covered until shaking stops
If a child is anxious: the helper reassures that most buildings do not collapse and that practising helps you feel ready
Praise naming a trusted adult and a short, clear message to tell them
activities.rationale: A calm helper persona can coach the steps, address worries and secure the 'tell a trusted adult' habit. Talking through the steps supports recall and reassurance; it does not itself elicit the physical performance, so use it to supplement the drill.
sourceClaims: Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Respond to a friendly safety helper who asks 'What would you do first if the ground shook?'
Talk through each step aloud as the helper coaches: drop, cover, hold on
Say who your trusted adult is and what you would tell them afterwards
Ask the helper any worries, and hear the reassurance that most buildings do not collapse
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearses recalling and explaining the routine and names a trusted adult, keeping the tone calm and reassuring.

constraints: The real learning objective is embodied muscle memory: a teacher-led physical drill with a real desk where children actually drop, cover and hold on is the primary activity. On-screen rehearsals, sorting tasks, labelled images and helper dialogue are scaffolds/primers that teach the sequence and reasoning but do not rehearse the physical moves.

Sequencing, sorting and choose-the-reason formats verify recognition and recall of the steps and myths; they do not elicit the fast, timed physical response, so do not treat them as proof a child can perform the drill under pressure.
Teach children to act immediately rather than freeze, and to choose a sturdy table/desk as cover — not just any spot, since not all spots give equal protection from falling objects.
Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact throughout — this is preparedness, not fear. Always reassure that most buildings do not collapse.
Always end any rehearsal by naming a trusted adult to tell; have each child name theirs.
This topic teaches a rehearsable safety response only, not earthquake causes. Do not drift into explaining why earthquakes happen.
Teach 'hold on until the shaking fully stops' — shaking can pause and restart; leaving cover during a pause is unsafe.

Myths to confront with simple reasons: 'run outside' (moving during shaking can make you fall, and the area near exterior walls and windows is most dangerous), 'stand in a doorway' (not stronger in modern buildings and gives no protection from falling or flying objects), 'just hide anywhere' (needs sturdy cover) and 'freeze and wait' (act immediately). Avoid the discredited 'triangle of life' advice.
This is a preparedness/life-skill, not an England National Curriculum science/geography topic; its closest UK home is PSHE/personal safety. It is also not a stand-alone NGSS performance expectation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that most injuries come from falling/flying objects (not collapse) and the 'do not run outside / doorway not safest' guidance reflect the cited Earthquake Country Alliance (and USGS/FEMA-aligned) advice for typical modern, building-code-compliant structures. These recommendations can vary by building type and region; treat them as the standard guidance presented, not as universal across all structures.

The pedagogy's framing that the on-screen activities do not build true bodily reflex, and that physical practice is 'the point', is retained as the stated objective. The superiority of a physical drill over screen rehearsal for building reflex is an expert-stated rationale in the source material, not independently verified comparative efficacy here; it is presented as a narrow affordance (the drill rehearses the actual moves) rather than a proven head-to-head result.
The UK (PSHE) and US (not an NGSS performance expectation) standards framing comes from a source marked unverified in the row; retained as context, not as a verified claim.

probeDeeper: Why did you get under the table instead of standing by the window?
The shaking pauses for a second — do you get up now or stay put? Why?
After the shaking stops, who would you tell, and what would you say?
Why is running out of the door while it's still shaking not the safest choice?
assess.correctAnswer: The child immediately DROPS to hands and knees, takes COVER under the sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows and shelves), and HOLDS ON until the shaking stops — staying put rather than running outside or to a doorway — and afterwards says they'd tell a trusted adult.

errorPatterns.pattern: Runs outside as soon as the shaking starts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the words — model that the most dangerous place is next to exterior walls and windows; stay and take cover until shaking stops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Heads for the door or outdoors the moment shaking begins.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stands in a doorway to be safe (outdated advice)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Doorways aren't safer in modern buildings; get down under a sturdy table.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Goes to a doorway instead of getting under cover.

errorPatterns.pattern: Freezes or stays standing near windows and shelves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the drop-cover-hold sequence; falling and flying objects are the main danger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stays upright beside hazards; doesn't drop or cover.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops and covers but lets go or crawls out before the shaking stops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold on and stay put until it's fully over — shaking can pause and start again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves cover during a pause in the shaking.

responseLevels.gap: Freezes, runs outside, or heads to a doorway/window; doesn't drop or take cover.
responseLevels.full: Promptly drops, covers under sturdy shelter away from windows and shelves, and holds on until shaking stops (not running out or to a doorway), and explains it's because of falling objects — naming a trusted adult to tell afterwards.
responseLevels.partial: Performs part of the sequence (e.g. drops and covers) but lets go early or hesitates about running outside, and can't fully explain why to stay away from windows.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Let's pretend the ground has just started shaking hard, right now. Show me exactly what you would do, from the moment you feel it until the shaking stops. (Set the room up with a sturdy table, a window, and some shelves.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite 'drop, cover, hold on' yet, when actually acting, run to the window or door or stand in a doorway. Watching the movements — and where they go — separates knowing the words from performing the safe procedure; running outside and heading for a doorway are the documented unsafe responses.
